newsitem.title: UK: Early winter chill reignites oil price rally.
newsitem.headline: Early winter chill reignites oil price rally.

text.p: An early cold snap has reignited a blistering oil price rally that is fuelling fears of global inflation as oil companies rush to raise low heating fuel stocks before winter demand in the northern hemisphere really bites.

World benchmark Brent crude oil futures for December were valued at $23.80 per barrel on Thursday, just over a dollar below October's six-year high of $25.06 and well above an early-November low of $22.11.

The rise in world oil prices was a chilling reminder to consumers of the risks of running down their stocks ahead of winter, and oil traders said more hard lessons may be in store before the end of the year.
Many believe that prices will return to six-year highs of $25 per barrel within the next six weeks, reviving the inflationary spectre.

"Our perception is that this market should firm. The weather is getting colder on both sides of the Atlantic, and all the forecasts say it will get colder still," said Michel Bernard, an oil trading manager at Shell UK. "I would not be surprised if Brent hit $25 per barrel again before the end of the year."
So far this year, oil prices have averaged $3.00 per barrel above 1995.
October's rally was triggered by signs that European and U.S. stocks of heating oil, also known as distillates, were dangerously low ahead of winter.

In the world's biggest oil user, the United States, stocks fell again last week, according to Wednesday's data from the American Petroleum Institute (API). Inventories were 14 million barrels below last year, and all of this shortfall was concentrated in the key heating oil consuming region of the northeast, the data showed.
"We're one week closer to winter and distillate stocks fell. I believe we're setting up for another rally in distillates," said Tom Knight, a U.S.-based trader with Belgian oil company Fina Inc.
The trend was mirrored in Europe, where distillate stocks at the end of October were 22 million barrels below last year, according to the Euroilstock Foundation.

"There are low stocks in the United States, low stocks in Europe, and on top of that the weather is cold and demand is getting stronger. Our expectation is that this market should come up," Shell's Bernard added.
High oil prices will not only raise winter fuel bills for consumers; economists say their inflationary impact could also derail Europe's moves towards monetary union.
"It is a risk reather than a forecast," said Ian McCafferty, director of international economics at NatWest Capital Markets in London.

"In Europe it provides one of the major risks that all of the script in the run-up to the Maastrict Treaty could go wrong. If we get an external shock that both depresses GDP and raises inflation, it poses quite a big policy dilemma for the authorities, particularly the (German) Bundesbank," he said of strict criteria for the European Union's economic and monetary union (EMU) which members are expected to meet in 1997.
